notes.meaning: Ezekiel looks up and sees what looks like a throne made of shining blue sapphire above the heads of the cherubim. The throne shows that the Lord is the supreme King over all heavenly beings and earthly powers. He sits in majesty, ready to direct everything according to His holy will.

The Lord tells the man clothed in linen to go between the whirling wheels beneath the cherubim, gather burning coals, and scatter them over Jerusalem. This burning action shows that the coming destruction of the city is an act of holy judgment from God. The same messenger who marked the faithful for safety is now sent to announce fiery judgment on the unrepentant.

The cherubim stand on the south side of the temple as the man goes in, and a thick cloud fills the inner courtyard. While a cloud often represents God's special presence, here it also signals His displeasure with the sin in His house. The cherubim wait in place, ready to assist in carrying out the Lord's holy purpose.

The bright glory of the Lord rises from above the cherubim and moves to the doorway of the temple. The inside of the temple becomes dark with the cloud, while the courtyard fills with the dazzling brightness of God's glory. God takes His stand at the threshold like a judge, pausing before He fully departs.

The beating wings of the cherubim make a sound so loud that people can hear it all the way out in the outer courtyard. It sounds like thunder, which the Scriptures often compare to the voice of God Almighty speaking. The roar serves as an alarming warning that God is preparing to move.

The man dressed in linen obeys the Lord's command and steps beside the wheels under the cherubim. One of the cherubim reaches into the fire between them, places hot coals directly into the man's hands, and the man goes out to scatter them. This shows the angels working in perfect harmony with God's servant to carry out His judgment.

Ezekiel notices the shape of human hands under the wings of the cherubim. These hands show that the heavenly creatures have great skill, readiness, and ability to carry out whatever tasks God gives them. They do not act on their own, but use their strength under God's guidance.

Four sparkling wheels sit beside the cherubim, with one wheel next to each creature, shining like a precious beryl stone. The wheels represent the turning events of this world and how God's providence guides history. Even when life feels unstable, God's wise care controls every turn.

All four wheels look exactly alike, appearing like one wheel set inside another at right angles. This design allows them to move instantly in any direction without hesitation. Though God's workings in the world can look tangled or confusing to us, all His plans fit together in perfect order.

When the wheels roll, they move straight forward in any direction without having to turn around. They simply follow whichever direction the front creature faces. This steady movement shows that God's plans go straight to their goal without being thrown off course.

The entire bodies, backs, hands, and wings of the cherubim, along with the rims of the wheels, are covered all over with eyes. These eyes show God's complete knowledge, wisdom, and constant watchfulness over everything that happens. Nothing in the world takes place by blind chance, because God sees and directs every single part.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase describing the bodies of the cherubim is missing from the ancient Greek translation and may have been added later to clarify the picture.

notes.meaning: A voice calls out to the wheels, giving them a command to start whirling into motion. The call sets the whole chariot mechanism moving together swiftly under God's direction. All creation stands ready to obey immediately whenever the Lord gives the word.

Each cherub has four faces: the face of a cherub, a human, a lion, and an eagle. These faces reflect the finest qualities found in God's creatures, such as wisdom, boldness, and swiftness. Where Ezekiel earlier saw the face of an ox, he now recognizes it as the special form of a cherub.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that this verse is not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts, and several modern Bible versions translate the first face as an ox to match Ezekiel's opening vision.

notes.meaning: The cherubim rise up into the air as Ezekiel watches. He recognizes right away that these are the very same living beings he had seen earlier by the Kebar River in Babylon. Seeing this familiar vision reassures him that the God who spoke to him in exile is the same God now acting in Jerusalem.

Whenever the cherubim move, the wheels roll right alongside them, and when the creatures spread their wings to lift off, the wheels stay right at their side. When the creatures stand still, the wheels stop, because the spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels. Every part of God's chariot works in complete unison to fulfill His divine purpose.

The glory of the Lord leaves the threshold of the temple and takes its place above the cherubim on the chariot. God prepares to leave His sanctuary because the people have defiled it with their sins. His slow and step-by-step movement shows how patient and reluctant He is to abandon His house.

The cherubim lift their wings and rise from the ground, with the wheels rolling along right beside them. They pause at the entrance of the eastern gate of the Lord's house, with God's glorious presence resting above them. By stopping at the outer gateway, the Lord pauses one more time before leaving the city entirely.

Ezekiel confirms again that these were the living creatures he saw beneath the God of Israel by the Kebar River. Now that he sees them in the temple, he understands clearly that they are cherubim. This confirmed to him that the faithful covenant God is the one directing every part of this vision.

Ezekiel repeats that each cherub had four faces, four wings, and what looked like human hands under their wings. Repeating these details helped convince the stubborn exiles that what the prophet saw was true and dependable. God's angelic servants possess everything they need to carry out His commands swiftly.

Their faces look just like the faces Ezekiel saw by the Kebar River, and each creature moves straight forward without turning aside. Their steady, focused motion shows that nothing can distract or stop God's servants from doing His work. When the Lord sets His purpose in motion, it is carried through to the very end.
